(p-200) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This surah is Meccan.

﴿All praise is due to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers having wings, two or three or four. He increases in creation what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿Whatever Allah grants to people of mercy, none can withhold; and whatever He withholds, none can release thereafter. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿O mankind, remember the favor of Allah upon you. Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? There is no deity except Him, so how are you deluded?﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, [O Muhammad], already were messengers denied before you. And to Allah are returned all matters.﴾ ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life delude you, and let not the Deceiver delude you concerning Allah.﴾

"Fatir" means "creator" (khaliq), but it adds to the meaning the sense of being alone in initiating its creation. From this is the saying of the Bedouin: "Ana fatartuha" (I originated it), meaning: I began digging it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I did not understand the meaning of 'Fatir' until I heard the saying of the Bedouin." Al-Zuhri recited: "al-hamdu lillahi fatara." Most of the people recited "jail" (originator/maker) in the genitive, and a group recited "jA'iluhu" in the nominative, as a cut from the attribute. Khalid ibn Nashit recited "ja'ala" in the past tense form, with "al-mala'ikata" in the accusative (p-201). As for this last reading, "rusulan" is in the accusative as the second object. As for the two earlier readings, it is said that "ja'il" is meant in the sense of the future, because the decree is from eternity, and the tanwin was dropped for lightness, and it acted in the manner of the future on "rusulan." A group said: "ja'il" carries the sense of the past, and "rusulan" is in the accusative by an implied verb, and "rusulan" means: by revelation and other commands. So Jibril, Mika'il, 'Izra'il and Israfil are messengers, and the angels who follow one another are messengers, and those who guide the rulers of justice are messengers, and others. Al-Hasan recited "rusulan" with a sukun on the sin.

"Ulī" is the plural of "dhū" (possessor), and from it: "al-taqiyyu dhu nuhyah" (the pious one possesses restraint), and "al-qawmu ulu nuhan." It is related from al-Hasan that he said, interpreting the saying of Maryam, peace be upon her: ﴿If you are fearing Allah﴾ [Maryam: 18]: Maryam knew that the pious one is one possessing restraint.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Mathna wa-thula'a wa-rubā'﴾ are words derived by alteration (ma'dulah) from "ithnayn," "thalatha," and "arba'a." They were altered in the indefinite state and thus became definite by the alteration, so they are not declined because of the alteration and the definiteness. It is said: because of the alteration and the attributive sense. The benefit of the alteration is to indicate repetition, because "mathna" is equivalent to your saying: "ithnayn ithnayn" (two by two). Qatada said: the kinds of angels are like this: some of them have two wings, some have three, some have four, and some exceed that, and it is related that Jibril, peace be upon him, has six hundred wings, two of which span from the east to the west. A group said: the meaning is that each side of the angel has two wings, and for some of them there are four. Otherwise, if each had three, they would not be balanced in the customary form of wings that we have seen. It is said: rather, each has three, like the fish. And Allah knows best.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ is an affirmation of what falls upon souls of wonder and amazement at the report of the angels with wings. That is: this is not a novelty in the power of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted; for He increases in His creation what He wills. It is related from al-Hasan and Ibn Shihab that they both said: the increase is beauty of voice. Al-Haytham al-Farisi said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream, and he said to me: 'You are al-Haytham who beautifies the Qur'an with your voice; may Allah reward you with good.'" It is also said: the increase is fine handwriting. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: « "Fine handwriting increases the truth in clarity." » Qatada (p-202) said: the increase is the beauty of the eyes. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verse 6–8:

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the blaze.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment, and those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so he sees it as good [equal to one who is guided]? Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So do not let yourself be consumed with regret over them. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Satan﴾ (verse)... It strengthens the reading of the one who read "al-Ghurur" with a fatha on the ghayn. His saying: ﴿so take him as an enemy﴾ means: by opposing him, cutting off from him, and differing from him by following the Sharia. Al-hizb (the party): the entourage and the followers. The lam in "liyakunu" (that they may be) is the lam of consequence (lam al-sayarura), because he did not invite them to the blaze; rather, it happened that their affair ended, as a result of his calling them, in that. Al-sa'ir is one of the levels of Hell, and it has seven levels.

His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ is in the place of nominative case by way of the inceptive (mubtada'). This is the better view, because of the conjunction of "those who believe" (alladhina amanu) upon it afterwards; thus they are two balanced sentences. Some people allowed that "alladhina" be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yakunu", and another allowed that it be in the place of the genitive case as a substitute for "ashab", and this is possible, but the inceptive is more preponderant.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is one for whom﴾ (verse)... It is an interrogation (tawqif), and its answer is omitted. Its estimate, according to al-Kisa'i, is: "his soul goes to waste in regret over him." It is possible to estimate: "like one who was guided," and similar estimates. The best of them is what the wording after it indicates. Talha read "amman" without a fa'. This verse is a consolation to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, regarding the disbelief of his people. It is obligatory to submit to Allah, the Exalted, regarding His misguiding whom He wills and guiding whom He wills, and He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from their affair, and not to let himself perish out of grief over them. Al-Hasan read "tadhhaba" with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', "nafsuka" in the nominative case. Abu Ja'far, Qatada, 'Isa, and al-Ashhab read "tudhhib" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', "nafsaka" in the accusative case, and it was also transmitted from Nafi'. Al-hasra (regret): the distress of the soul over the loss of a matter. Ibn Zayd cited for this his saying: ﴿lest a soul say, "Oh, my regret over what I neglected"﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]. Then he threatened the disbelievers with his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verses 9–10:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and bring the earth to life with it after its death. Such is the Resurrection.﴾ ﴿Whoever desires honour, then to Allah belongs all honour. To Him ascend the good word, and righteous deed raises it. As for those who plot evil deeds, there is a severe punishment for them, and the plotting of those will come to nothing.﴾

This is an argument against the disbelievers who denied the resurrection from the graves. Allah, the Exalted, pointed them to the example they witness, which is equivalent to the bringing to life of the dead. The "dead land" is that which has no vegetation, having become dusty from drought. When water from the clouds reaches it, it turns green and produces plants, and that is its life. "Nushur" is a verbal noun from nashara, meaning the dead one came back to life. From it comes the saying of al-A'sha:

﹡ "How strange is the dead man who rises!"

(p-205) As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾, it may bear three meanings. The first is: whoever desires honour through domination, then to Allah belongs honour, meaning it is not for anyone else and cannot be complete except for Him. This seeker of domination is dominated. Mujahid took this view and said: whoever desires honour through the worship of idols.

The Qadi (judge) Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an appeal to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they might be for them a source of honour﴾ [Maryam: 81].

The second meaning: whoever desires honour and its upright path, and loves to attain it in its proper manner, then to Allah belongs honour, meaning through Him and by His command. His honour is not attained except through obedience to Him. Qatadah took this view.

The third meaning, which al-Farra' stated: whoever desires knowledge of honour, then to Allah belongs honour, meaning He is the one characterised by it. "Jami'an" (all) is a circumstantial accusative (hal).

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him ascend the good word﴾, that is, the declaration of Divine unity (tawhid), glorification (tamjid), the remembrance of Allah, and the like. al-Dahhak recited "yusʻadu" with a dammah on the ya' (yuṣʻadu, passive), and the majority recited "al-kalim", which is the plural of kalimah (word). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman recited "al-kalam" (speech). "Al-tayyib" (good) is that whose hearing is pleasing in a legally sanctioned way (al-istihsan al-shar'i). Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, and Allah is greatest" have a humming around the Throne like the buzzing of bees, which mention their speaker.

(p-206) As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And righteous deed raises it﴾, people differed regarding the pronoun: to what does it refer? One group said it refers to "the deed". This group then differed: some said the subject of "yarfa'u" (raises) is "the word", meaning the righteous deed is raised by the word, which is the statement "la ilaha illa Allah", since no deed is raised except with tawhid. Others said the verb is ascribed to Allah, the Exalted, meaning it is He who raises the righteous deed, and this is the most preferred view.

Ibn 'Abbas, Shahr ibn Hawshab, Mujahid and Qatadah said: the pronoun in "yarfa'uhu" refers to "the word", meaning it is the righteous deed that raises the word. The expressions of the proponents of this view differed. Some of them said: it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when the servant remembers Allah, the Exalted, and says a good word, and performs his obligatory duties, his word is raised along with his deed; and when he speaks but does not perform his obligations, his word is rejected back upon his deed. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verses 9–10:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and bring the earth to life with it after its death. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then He made you into pairs. No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And none is granted a long life, nor is any of his life shortened, except that it is in a Book. Indeed that is easy for Allah.﴾

This verse is a reminder of the attributes of Allah, may He be exalted, in the manner of what preceded it. This discourse concerns the idols and the resurrection of bodies from the graves. The Exalted said: "created you from dust," meaning from the time He created Adam, our father, peace be upon him, from it. ﴿Then from a sperm-drop﴾, meaning by procreation from the semen of men. As for "pairs" (azwaj), it was said: its meaning is "kinds" (anwa'), and it was said: it means the marriage of men to women.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And none is granted a long life﴾, the verse... people have differed concerning the return of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿nor is any of his life shortened﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, and others said that its implication is that it refers back to ﴿"mu'ammar"﴾, which is a noun of genus, and the intended meaning is other than the one who is granted long life. That is, the statement includes two persons: one of them is granted a life of a hundred years or so, and from the other is shortened, by being one year or so. This is the view of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, but it returned a pronoun for the sake of brevity and conciseness. The complete explanation would be to say: "nor is any of the life of one granted long life shortened," because the word ﴿"mu'ammar"﴾ is in the position of "one who has a life," as if he said: "none is granted long life from one who has a life, nor is the life of one who has a life shortened."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, also said, as did Abu Malik and Ibn Jubayr: the intended meaning is a single person, and the pronoun refers to him, i.e., no person is granted a long life nor is his life shortened, by counting what has passed of it: when a year passes, that is recorded, then another year, and this is the shortening. Ibn Jubayr said: what has passed of his life is the shortening, and what is yet to come is what He grants him. It is narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: the meaning is: nor is his life shortened, i.e., he is not cut off by the power of Allah, the Exalted, and if He willed, He would have delayed that cause. It is also narrated that he said when 'Umar, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, was stabbed: "If he had prayed to Allah, the Exalted, He would have increased his term." The Muslims denied this from him and said: Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour﴾ [al-A'raf: 34], and he argued with this verse. This is a weak, rejected view, which implies the doctrine of two terms (ajalayn), and the Mu'tazilah adhered to something similar to it.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Ibn Sirin read "yanqusu" with the verb in the active voice, i.e., Allah diminishes. Al-Hasan and Dawud read "min 'umrihi" with the mim sukun. The Book mentioned in the verse is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). His saying: ﴿Indeed that﴾ refers to the determination of these lifespans and the reckoning of their details and hours.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verse 12:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, pleasant to drink, and this one is salty, bitter. And from each you eat fresh flesh and extract ornaments which you wear, and you see the ships plowing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful.﴾

This is another verse by which every person of intellect reasons, and he is certain that no idol has any part in it. By "the two seas" (al-bahrān) he means the entirety of salt water and the entirety of sweet water wherever it is, so he means by it the totality of this and the totality of that. "Furāt" (sweet, sweetest) is that which is extremely sweet, and "ujāj" is that which is extremely salty, to the point that its saltiness borders on bitterness. Al-Rummānī said: it is from ajjajtu al-nār (I kindled the fire), as if it burns with its heat. 'Īsā al-Thaqafī read sayyigh sharābuhu without an alif and with a doubled yā', and Ṭalḥa read malih with a fatḥa on the mīm and a kasra on the lām.

"Fresh flesh" is fish, which exists in both seas, and likewise the ships travel in both seas. There remain the ornaments, which are pearls and coral. Al-Zajjāj and others said: this expression implies that the ornaments come out of both of them, whereas they only come out of the salt water, and that is permissible, as He said in another verse: ﴿From both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 22], and as He said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'ām: 130], while the messengers are only from humankind.

Some people said: rather, the ornaments come out of both seas. This is because the oyster of the pearl is, so they claim, reached by rainwater, so some of it is extracted and the gem is found in it, and some of it splits open in the sea at its death and cuts it, and its gem comes out by thirst and other devices. This is from the sweet water, so the bringing forth is attributed to it because of what occurs of the ornament through a cause. Also, the entire sweet sea pours into the salt sea, so the bringing forth comes from both of them together. Abū Dhu'ayb was faulted for his saying in describing the gem:

❁ So he brought her, whatever you wish, of Lṭimī quality, / upon whose face the water of the Furāt surges.

This is not an error according to what we have mentioned of the interpretation of this group.

"Al-fulk" in this place is a plural, by the evidence of its being described with a plural.

"Mawākhir" is the plural of mākhira, which is that which ploughs the water, i.e., cuts through it. It was also said: the mākhira is that which cuts through the wind, and then a sound arises; and al-makhr is the sound that arises from the ship's movement by the wind. The exegetes expressed this with expressions that are not specific to the word. Some of them said: the mawākhir are those that go and come with one wind. Mujāhid said: the wind ploughs the ships, and the ships do not plough the wind except the great ships. Thus his wording occurs in al-Bukhārī, but the correct view is that al-fulk is the mākhira, not the makhūra.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿[li-tabtaghū]﴾ means for trade, pilgrimage, military campaign, and every journey that has a legitimate (sharʿī) aspect.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verses 13–14:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day, and He causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a qiṭmīr.﴾ ﴿If you invoke them, they do not hear your call; and even if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association (of them with Allah). And none can inform you like the One who is All-Aware.﴾

﴿"Yūliju"﴾ means "He causes to enter" (yudkhilu). This is an expression meaning that what is lost from the night is added to the day, as if it had entered into it; likewise, what is lost from the day enters into the night. The alif and lam in ﴿al-shamsa wa-l-qamara﴾ (the sun and the moon) are for specificity (al-ʿahd, previously known reference). It has also been said that they are superfluous, having neither meaning nor definiteness; and this is the correct view. The "specified term" (al-ajal al-musammā) is the establishment of the Hour (qiyām al-sāʿa). It has also been said that it refers to the durations of the night and the durations of the day; on this view, "ajal" is a noun of genus (ism jins). The majority of reciters read "tadʿūna" with the letter tāʾ, while al-Ḥasan and Yaʿqūb read it with the letter yāʾ. The "qiṭmīr" is the thin skin that lies over the date-stone; this is the saying of the people of knowledge (al-nās al-ḥujja), while Juwaybir reported from his narrators that the qiṭmīr is the cup-like cap at the top of the date, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the first view is more well-known and more correct.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, explained the matter of the idols with three things, each of which indicates their falsehood. The first is that they do not hear when they are called upon; the second is that they do not respond even if they were to hear; and the reason He mentioned this is that a far-fetched speaker might say: "Perhaps they hear." The third is that they disown the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection.

And ﴿yakfurūna bi-shirkikum﴾ means: by their having made them partners with Allah. He attributed the association (shirk) to them because they are the ones who established it; thus it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the genitive construction with the agent. The phrase ﴿yakfurūna﴾ may be understood as speech and expression which Allah grants to the idols and creates in them an understanding that entails it; or it may be understood as what becomes apparent there of their stillness and silence at the movement of every speaker and the rebuttal of every arguer. This latter is then in the manner of metaphor (tajawwuz), as Dhu al-Rumma said:

I stood at the abode of Mayya, which speaks; its traces address me and I address it.
And I watered it until, from what I poured out, [...] its stones and its playgrounds speak to me.

As for Allah's saying, ﴿and none can inform you like the One who is All-Aware﴾, the exegetes, Qatada and others, said: by "the All-Aware" He intends Himself; He is the All-Aware, the one whose report is true, and He has reported this, so there is no doubt about its occurrence. It is also possible that the saying ﴿and none can inform you like the One who is All-Aware﴾ is a continuation of the mention of the idols, as if He said: none informs you like one who informs about himself, and they have informed about themselves by disbelieving in these (who worshipped them).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verses 15–18:

The words of the Most High:

﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation.﴾ ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah.﴾ ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a near relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord in the unseen and establish the prayer. Whoever purifies himself, purifies only for his own soul. And to Allah is the final return.﴾

This is a verse of admonition and reminder. The human being is in need of Allah, the Most High, in the minutest and the greatest of matters. He cannot be independent of Him for the blink of an eye, while He is independent of every one of them. Allah, the Most High, is free of need of people and of all His creatures; He is Self-Sufficient absolutely. *Al-Hamid* (the Praiseworthy) means the One who is praised absolutely. His words ﴿"bi-'azīz"﴾ mean: "by anything that could be prevented" (i.e., nothing can thwart Him).

*Tazir* means: bears a heavy burden. This verse concerns sins, transgressions and crimes. This is the view of Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Its occasion of revelation was that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to some of the believers: "Disbelieve in Muhammad, and I will bear your burden." So Allah, the Most High, ruled that no one bears the burden of another. As for those rulers who resorted to seizing a relative for the crime of another relative, like the action of Ziyad and the like, the reason is that the one seized may have helped the criminal through support and association, or through knowing about his condition and approving of it. Thus he has taken a share of the crime. This is the meaning of the words of the Most High: ﴿And they will surely carry their own burdens and other burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13], because they led them astray. This is also the meaning of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever establishes a bad practice, he bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it after him, and whoever establishes a good practice, he has its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it after him."

The feminine form ﴿"wāziratun"﴾ is used because it is treated in the sense of "soul" (nafs). On this basis ﴿"muthqalatun"﴾ is also made feminine. *Al-hmil* (the load) is what is on the back in the case of physical objects, and it is used figuratively for meanings such as sins and the like. Thus every burden is treated as attached to the back, just as every acquisition is attributed to the hand. The subject of *kāna* (the grammatical subject of "was") is a pronoun implied in the sentence, its estimated form being: "even if the one being called were..."

Then the Most High informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that he only warns those who have fear, and they are the ones who are granted knowledge; that is, only they benefit from the warning. Otherwise, He sent him to warn the whole world.

His words ﴿"bil-ghayb"﴾ mean: while He is absent from them; He is only a messenger. Then He specified establishing the prayer from among the deeds, as a reminder of it and an honouring of it.

Then the Most High, glorified is He, urged purification, by holding out to it the utmost hope. Talhah recited: "Whoever purifies himself (wa-man izzakkā), he purifies only for himself (fa-innamā yazzakkā li-nafsih)." Then after that He warned with His words: ﴿And to Allah is the final return.﴾

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Every expression falls short of explaining the eloquence of this verse, and so is the whole Book of Allah. But the matter becomes clear to us in some places more than in others, according to the extent of our shortcomings.

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colours? The sight in His words ﴿"Have you not seen"﴾ is sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb, sight of the mind), and every mention of seeing in the Qur'an is sight of the heart, because proof is established by it. But sight of the heart is never formed except upon a sense, so sometimes the sense is sight of the eyes, and sometimes it is other than that, and this is known according to the thing being spoken of. And "anna" (that) stands in place of the two objects of the verb of seeing; this is the view of Sibawayh, because "anna" with what follows it is a clause. This does not apply in your saying "ra'aytu" (I saw) and "zanantu dhalika" (I thought that), because your saying "dhalika" is not a clause as "anna" is. The view of al-Zajjaj is that the second object is omitted, its implied sense being: "Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky as truth?" And he shifted from address with mention of the third person to the first person with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), because it is more awe-inspiring in expression.

(p-216) His words ﴿"varying colours"﴾ may mean yellow, red, white, black and other than these, and the continuous mention of these colours afterwards supports this. It may also mean kinds (al-anwa'), and the counted item in this interpretation is greater in number.

"Judad" is the plural of "judda," which is a streak that occurs in the land and the mountain, like a great piece continuous in length. From it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"As though his back's spine and streak of his back were / Beads among which a shining flows (dalis)."

Abu 'Ubayda related in some of his books that it is said "judad" is the plural of "jadid" (new), but the meaning of "new" has no place in this verse. al-Zuhri read it as [jadad] with a fatha on the jim.

His words ﴿"and intensely black"﴾: the two words are for one meaning. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah dislikes the elderly man who dyes his hair black" — that is, the one who dyes with black. He put the more eloquent description first, though its proper place was later, and it is the same in meaning; but the eloquent speech of the Arabs often comes in this manner.

His words ﴿"varying in colours"﴾: before it there is an omitted noun to which the pronoun refers; its implied sense is: "and among the livestock is a kind varying in its colours." "Dawabb" (moving creatures) includes people and livestock, but both are mentioned as a reminder of them. His words ﴿"Thus"﴾ may be part of the first speech, so a pause upon it is good, and many of the exegetes went to this; and it may be part of the second speech, coming out as a cause, as if he said: "Just as power has come in all of this, only those of knowledge among His servants fear Allah," that is, those who gather these lessons and reflect upon them. Some exegetes said: "Fear is the head of knowledge," but this is a preachy expression that does not hold up under critical examination. Rather, the correct and consistent view is that knowledge is the head of fear and its cause. What is reported from the Prophet ﷺ is that he said: "The fear of Allah is the head of all wisdom," and he said: "The head of wisdom is the fear of Allah." This is the clear statement. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Asceticism is sufficient as knowledge." Masruq said: "It is sufficient knowledge for a person that he fears Allah." And the Exalted said: ﴿"He who fears will be reminded"﴾ [al-A'la: 10]. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "The most knowledgeable of you about Allah is the most fearful of Him." al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "Whoever does not fear Allah is not a scholar." It is said that the opening of the Zabur is: "The head of wisdom is the fear of Allah." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Fear of Allah is sufficient as knowledge, and being deceived by it is ignorance." Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: "The scholar is only one who fears Allah." And [innama] in this verse is for specifying the scholars, not for exclusivity (hasr); it is a particle that may signify exclusivity, and it also comes without it. This is known only according to the meaning in which it occurs. So when you say: "The brave one is only 'Antara," and you say: "Allah is only one God," the difference becomes clear to you, so reflect on it.

This verse in its entirety is evidence of God's oneness and power, and its aim is to establish proof against the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verses 32–34:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those whom We chose from among Our servants. Some of them wrong themselves, some are moderate, and some are foremost in good deeds, by Allah's permission. That is the great bounty.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they will say: "All praise is for Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative."﴾

(p-219) ﴿"Awrathna" (We caused to inherit)﴾ means: We gave it to one group after the death of another group. Inheritance, whether literal or figurative, is only said of what comes to a person after another's death. Here, "the Book" is intended to mean the meanings of the Book, its knowledge, its rulings and its beliefs. So when Allah, the Exalted, gave the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ the Qur'an, which comprises the meanings of the books revealed before it, it is as if He made the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ inherit the Book that was among the nations before them.

By ﴿those whom We chose﴾ is meant the Ummah of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others. The wording may seem to include all believers of every nation, but the expression "giving the Book as an inheritance" applies only to the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, and the earlier nations did not inherit it. "Istafayna" means: We chose and preferred. "Al-'Ibad" (the servants) is general, covering the whole world, both its believers and its disbelievers.

People differed about what the pronoun in Allah's saying ﴿fa-minhum﴾ ("among them") refers to. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, held, as its implication, that the pronoun refers to "those" (alladhina), and that the three categories are all within the Ummah of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Thus "the one who wrongs himself" is the disobedient transgressor; "the moderate" is the one who avoids major sins, and this is the majority of the Ummah; and "the foremost" is the one who is God-fearing absolutely. This group said: the three categories are all in Paradise. This was also said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him. The pronoun in ﴿"yadkhulunaha"﴾ (they will enter it) refers to the three categories. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: they all entered Paradise. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "By the Lord of the Ka'ba, their shoulders are level, and they differ only in their deeds"; in another narration: "their shoulders rub against one another." Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i said: "As for what I have heard for sixty years, all of them are saved." Ibn Mas'ud said: On the Day of Resurrection this Ummah will be in three groups: a third will enter Paradise without reckoning, a third will be reckoned with an easy reckoning and then enter Paradise, and a third will come with great sins. Allah will say: "What are these?"—and He knows them best—so the angels will say: "They are sinners, but they did not associate anything with You." Then the Mighty and Majestic will say: "Admit them into the vastness of My mercy." 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said in the book of al-Tha'labi: The foremost is one who embraced Islam before the Hijra, the moderate is one who embraced it after it, and the wrongdoer is us. Al-Hasan said: The foremost is one whose good deeds outweigh his bad; the moderate is one whose good and bad are equal; and the wrongdoer is one whose scales are light. (p-220) Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: The foremost is the scholar, the moderate is the learner, and the wrongdoer is the ignorant. Dhu al-Nun said: The wrongdoer is the one who remembers Allah only with his tongue, the moderate is the one who remembers Him with his heart, and the foremost is the one who never forgets Him. Al-Antaki said: The wrongdoer is the possessor of words, the moderate is the possessor of deeds, and the foremost is the possessor of states. Usama ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said: "They are all in Paradise." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, recited this verse and then said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Our foremost is foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven." The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said: "I am the foremost of the Arabs, Salman is the foremost of the Persians, Suhayb is the foremost of the Romans, and Bilal is the foremost of the Abyssinians." He, peace be upon him, meant that these are the leaders of the foremost. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Our foremost are the people of jihad, our moderate are the people of our settled places, and our wrongdoers are the people of our desert, who do not attend congregation or Friday prayer."

'Ikrima, Qatada and al-Hasan said, as its implication, that the pronoun in "minhum" refers to "the servants" (al-'Ibad). The one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever and the hypocrite; the moderate is the believer who disobeys; and the foremost is the God-fearing absolutely. They said: this verse is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And you were three kinds of couples﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 7]. The pronoun in His saying ﴿"yadkhulunaha"﴾ according to this view is specific to the two groups: the moderate and the foremost, while the wrongdoing group is in the Fire. They said: it is far-fetched that one who wrongs himself should be among those chosen, as the first interpretation implies. This view was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Some scholars said: He mentioned the wrongdoer first because he relies only on the mercy of Allah. The moderate is the one who is balanced in his affairs, who does not go to excess in any direction, but keeps to the middle course. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The best of matters are their middle course."

A group said—there is no meaning to their saying—that Allah's saying ﴿those whom We chose﴾ refers to the prophets, and that the one among them who wrongs himself is one who fell into a minor sin. This view is rejected on many grounds.

The majority read ﴿"sabiqun bil-khayrat"﴾ (foremost in good deeds); Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read "sabbaq" (intensive form).

Allah's saying ﴿bi-idhnillah﴾ (by Allah's permission) means: by His command and His will, regarding whomever of His servants He loves. His saying ﴿That is the great bounty﴾ refers to the choosing and what results from it of mercy.

Al-Tabari said: the racing toward good deeds is the great bounty. In the book of al-Tha'labi, it is said: He gathered them all in entering Paradise because it is an inheritance, and the righteous and the disobedient child are equal in inheritance given valid lineage; likewise these, given valid faith.

The majority read "jannatu" (gardens) in the nominative, as an apposition to "al-fadl" (the bounty). Al-Jahdari read "jannati" in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb explained by ﴿"yadkhulunaha"﴾. Zirr ibn Hubaysh read "jannatu 'adnin" in the singular, (p-222) Abu 'Amr read "yudkhalunaha" in the passive voice, narrated also from Ibn Kathir; the rest read it with a fathah on the yaa' and a dammah on the kha'.

"Asawir" is the plural of "uswira," and "uswira" is the plural of "siwar," with the sin vowelled either with a dammah or a kasrah. In Ubayy's codex it is "asawir," the plural of "aswar," which is also said of ornaments; the well-known meaning of "aswar" is the skilled archers of the Persian army. "Yuhallawna" means: men and women alike. 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "wa-lu'lu'an" in the accusative, coordinated with "asawira." 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, used to read "walulu'an" with the first waw sukun without hamza and the second with hamza; the opposite was also narrated from him. The rest read "wa-lu'lu'in" with hamza and in the genitive, coordinated with "asawira."

"Al-Hazan" (grief) in this verse is general, covering all kinds of sorrow. The exegetes specified it here: Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the grief of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and what befalls one there from the distress and sorrow of one's own wronging. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it is the grief of Hell. 'Ata' said: the grief of death. Qatada said: the worldly grief of fear that their deeds will not be accepted. Other things have been said which are part of grief. There is no point in specifying any of these sorrows, since grief in its entirety has departed from them. Their saying ﴿"inna Rabbana laghafurun shakur"﴾ (indeed our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative) describes Him, blessed and exalted, as one who forgives sins and rewards small good deeds with great reward; and this is His thankfulness, there being no lord but Him.

By ﴿those whom We chose﴾ is meant the Ummah of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others. The wording may seem to include all believers of every nation, but the expression "giving the Book as an inheritance" applies only to the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, and the earlier nations did not inherit it. "Istafayna" means: We chose and preferred. "Al-'Ibad" (the servants) is general, covering the whole world, both its believers and its disbelievers.

People differed about what the pronoun in Allah's saying ﴿fa-minhum﴾ ("among them") refers to. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, held, as its implication, that the pronoun refers to "those" (alladhina), and that the three categories are all within the Ummah of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Thus "the one who wrongs himself" is the disobedient transgressor; "the moderate" is the one who avoids major sins, and this is the majority of the Ummah; and "the foremost" is the one who is God-fearing absolutely. This group said: the three categories are all in Paradise. This was also said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him. The pronoun in ﴿"yadkhulunaha"﴾ (they will enter it) refers to the three categories. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: they all entered Paradise. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "By the Lord of the Ka'ba, their shoulders are level, and they differ only in their deeds"; in another narration: "their shoulders rub against one another." Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i said: "As for what I have heard for sixty years, all of them are saved." Ibn Mas'ud said: On the Day of Resurrection this Ummah will be in three groups: a third will enter Paradise without reckoning, a third will be reckoned with an easy reckoning and then enter Paradise, and a third will come with great sins. Allah will say: "What are these?"—and He knows them best—so the angels will say: "They are sinners, but they did not associate anything with You." Then the Mighty and Majestic will say: "Admit them into the vastness of My mercy." 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said in the book of al-Tha'labi: The foremost is one who embraced Islam before the Hijra, the moderate is one who embraced it after it, and the wrongdoer is us. Al-Hasan said: The foremost is one whose good deeds outweigh his bad; the moderate is one whose good and bad are equal; and the wrongdoer is one whose scales are light. (p-220) Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: The foremost is the scholar, the moderate is the learner, and the wrongdoer is the ignorant. Dhu al-Nun said: The wrongdoer is the one who remembers Allah only with his tongue, the moderate is the one who remembers Him with his heart, and the foremost is the one who never forgets Him. Al-Antaki said: The wrongdoer is the possessor of words, the moderate is the possessor of deeds, and the foremost is the possessor of states. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, recited this verse and then said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Our foremost is foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven." The one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever and the hypocrite; the moderate is the believer who disobeys; and the foremost is the God-fearing absolutely. They said: this verse is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And you were three kinds of couples﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 7]. They said: it is far-fetched that one who wrongs himself should be among those chosen, as the first interpretation implies. This view was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The best of matters are their middle course."

The majority read ﴿"sabiqun bil-khayrat"﴾ (foremost in good deeds); Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read "sabbaq" (intensive form).

Allah's saying ﴿bi-idhnillah﴾ (by Allah's permission) means: by His command and His will, regarding whomever of His servants He loves. His saying ﴿That is the great bounty﴾ refers to the choosing and what results from it of mercy.

Al-Tabari said: the racing toward good deeds is the great bounty. In the book of al-Tha'labi, it is said: He gathered them all in entering Paradise because it is an inheritance, and the righteous and the disobedient child are equal in inheritance given valid lineage; likewise these, given valid faith.

The majority read "jannatu" (gardens) in the nominative, as an apposition to "al-fadl" (the bounty). Al-Jahdari read "jannati" in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb explained by ﴿"yadkhulunaha"﴾. Zirr ibn Hubaysh read "jannatu 'adnin" in the singular, (p-222) Abu 'Amr read "yudkhalunaha" in the passive voice, narrated also from Ibn Kathir; the rest read it with a fathah on the yaa' and a dammah on the kha'.

"Asawir" is the plural of "uswira," and "uswira" is the plural of "siwar," with the sin vowelled either with a dammah or a kasrah. In Ubayy's codex it is "asawir," the plural of "aswar," which is also said of ornaments; the well-known meaning of "aswar" is the skilled archers of the Persian army. The rest read "wa-lu'lu'in" with hamza and in the genitive, coordinated with "asawira."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it is the grief of Hell. 'Ata' said: the grief of death. Qatada said: the worldly grief of fear that their deeds will not be accepted. Their saying ﴿"inna Rabbana laghafurun shakur"﴾ (indeed our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative) describes Him, blessed and exalted, as one who forgives sins and rewards small good deeds with great reward; and this is His thankfulness, there being no lord but Him.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 35, verses 35–37:**

God, the Exalted and Majestic, says:

﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty. No fatigue touches us therein, nor does weariness touch us therein.﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieved, for them is the fire of Hell. It will not be decreed upon them so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one.﴾ ﴿They will cry out therein: "Our Lord, bring us out, and we will do righteous deeds other than what we used to do." Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would be mindful could be mindful therein, and the warner came to you? So taste, for the wrongdoers have no helper.﴾

﴿"al-Muqamah"﴾: the *iqamah* (residence), from *aqama* (to dwell). *Al-maqamah*, with a fatha on the *mim*, means standing (*al-qiyam*), and it derives from *qama* (to stand). "Dar al-muqamah" is Paradise. *Al-nasab* is bodily exhaustion, and *al-lughub* is fatigue of the self (*nafs*) that follows from bodily exhaustion. Qatadah said: *al-lughub* means pain. The majority read "*lughubun*" with a damma on the *lam*. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) and al-Sulami read "*laghubun*" with a fatha on the *lam*, meaning something that wearies us. It may also be a verbal noun (*masdar*), like *al-wulugh* and *al-wudu'*.

Then God informs about the state of those who disbelieved, setting it in contrast to what He had mentioned earlier about those whom He chose. This supports the interpretation of those who said that the three categories are all in Paradise, since the mention of the disbelievers came here only. God's words ﴿They will not be decreed upon so that they die﴾ mean: they will not be finished off, because if they died their senses would cease and they would find rest. Al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Thaqafi read "*fayamutuna*" (so that they die), and its construction is coordination with "*yuqda*" (be decreed). This is a weak reading.

God's words ﴿Nor will its punishment be lightened for them﴾ are not contradicted by His words ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ (17:97), because the meaning is that the type of their punishment will not be lightened, and the type in itself admits of dying down or being kindled and the like. The majority read "*najzi*" with a nun and "*kulla*" in the accusative. Abu 'Amr, in one of the transmitted readings, read "*yujza*" with a dammed ya' as a passive verb, and "*kullu*" in the nominative.

"*Yastarikhuna*" is of the form *yaftaʿiluna*, from *al-sarakh* (crying out). Its original form is "*yastarikhuna*", then the *ta'* was changed to *ta'* (*tu'*), because the point of articulation of the *ta'* is close to that of the *sad*. In the speech there is an omitted element, which is estimated as: "Then it will be said to them: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough...?﴾" by way of rebuke and reproach. The *ma* in His words ﴿mа yatadhakkaru﴾ is temporal (*zarfiyyah*). People differed about the period which is for remembrance. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "Puberty," meaning that it is the first state of remembrance. Qatadah said: eighteen years. A group said: twenty years. Al-Zajjaj reported: seventeen years. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: forty years. This is a good view, and reports have been transmitted about it. It is also reported that when a servant reaches forty years and has not repented, Satan wipes over his face and says: "A face that will not prosper." Masruq ibn al-Ajda' said: Whoever reaches forty years should take his precaution against Allah. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When a man completes forty and has no modesty or veil beyond what is to come,*
*Leave him, and do not begrudge him what he has chosen, even if time drags the causes of life to him.*

Some people said that the limit is fifty, and from this the poet said:

*The brother of fifty, my strength has gathered, and vigor is in managing affairs.*

Another said:

*Indeed, a man who has lived fifty years is near to a watering place from its water.*

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) and others said: the limit in this is sixty, which is the age of excuse (*sinn al-i'dhar*). This too is a good and well-founded view. It is reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection it will be called out: Where are the sons of sixty?" This is the lifespan of which Allah said: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would be mindful could be mindful therein?﴾ And the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "Whoever Allah has granted a lifespan of sixty years has left him no excuse regarding his life."

The majority read ﴿"mā yatadhakkaru"﴾, and al-A'mash read "*mā yadhdhakkaru*" [*man idhdhakara*, meaning: whoever is mindful].

The *nadhir* (warner), according to the majority, is the prophets. Every prophet is a warner to his own community and to his contemporaries, and Muhammad (ﷺ) is the warner of the whole world throughout time. Al-Tabari said: "It was also said: the *nadhir* is white hair." This is a good view, except that the proof is established only by the legislated warning. The rest of the verse is clear.

[p. 226] The words of the Almighty:

﴿Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ ﴿It is He who made you successors upon the earth. So whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is upon himself, and the disbelief of the disbelievers increases them only in abhorrence with their Lord, and the disbelief of the disbelievers increases them only in loss.﴾ ﴿Say, "Have you considered your partners whom you invoke other than Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth, or do they have a partnership in the heavens? Or have We given them a Book so that they are upon clear evidence from it?" Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another only delusion.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease. And if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾

This is the beginning of a reminder of Allah, the Exalted, and evidence of His oneness and of His attributes, without which divinity would not be fitting. "Al-ghayb" (the unseen) is that which is hidden from humans. "Dhat al-sudur" (what is in the breasts) is what the breasts contain of beliefs and meanings. From this is the saying of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "The one who has in his belly the daughter of Kharijah," and from it is the saying of the Arabs: "The wolf is envied for his belly" (dhu batnihi), meaning for the puffed-up state within it, so whoever sees it thinks it is well-fed and recently ate.

"Khala'if" is the plural of "khalifah," like "safinah" with "safa'in," and "madinah" with "mada'in." The words of the Exalted: ﴿so upon himself is his disbelief﴾ contain an omitted modifier, its estimated meaning being: "upon himself is the burden of his disbelief and its harm." "Al-maqt" (abhorrence) is your contempt for a person because of his disobedience, or your hatred of the religion he adheres to. If the contempt is an unjust imposition from you, it is not called maqt. "Al-khasar" (loss) is a verbal noun from "khasira yakhsaru," meaning they lost their hereafter and their return, by going to the Fire and the punishment.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Have you considered your partners"﴾ and the verse that follows are an argument against the disbelievers regarding the invalidity of their idols. The Prophet ﷺ, by the command of their Lord, confronted them with their argument which they claimed was true. Then he confronted them, while the clear inability of them to create anything was evident, about the heavens: do they have a share in them? This too is evident after this. Then he confronted them: do they have a Book from Allah, the Exalted, that explains to them what they said? That is, all of that is not with them. Then, after this presumed denial, he turned to say: they only promise themselves delusion.

"A'aytum" (have you considered) functions, according to Sibawayh, in the position of "akhbirūni" (inform me), and therefore it does not require two objects. He attributed the partners to them in that they made them partners with Allah. That is, the idols have no partnership in any way except by your saying, so it is obligatory to attribute them to you. "Tad'una" (you invoke) means "ta'budūna" (you worship). The "ru'yah" (seeing) in the words of the Exalted ﴿"show me"﴾ is sight-seeing. "Al-shirk" is "al-sharikah" (partnership), also a verbal noun. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read [bayyinatin] in the plural. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, and Nafi' (with a variant from him) read "bayyinatin" in the singular, and the singular is meant as a plural, though it may be intended as singular. As you say: "I am upon clarity regarding this matter," or "upon clear evidence." Yet al-Mubarrad transmitted this as: "Qultu ṣāḥi qawwim."

And as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Fa-al-yawma ashrab ghayra mustaḥqibin / ithman mina Llāhi wa-lā wāghil"

("So today I drink, not bearing a sin from God, nor an uninvited intruder.")

Yet al-Mubarrad has transmitted it as: "Fa-al-yawma fa-ashrab."

("Travel on, sons of the paternal uncle, for al-Ahwāz is your dwelling, and the river Tīrā; the Arabs will not recognize you.")

"Yaḥīq" means: it surrounds, befalls, and descends upon. It is only used for what is disliked. His words, ﴿"illā bi-ahlihi"﴾, mean that it must befall them, either in this world or else in the Hereafter. Thus its corrupt consequence is theirs. Even if it sometimes befalls others in this world, its consequence falls on its own people.

Ka'b al-Aḥbār said to Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them both: "Indeed, in the Torah it says: 'Whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it.'" Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them both, replied: "I will show you this in the Book of God: ﴿'And evil scheming encompasses only its own people.'﴾"

"Yanẓurūna" means: they await. "Al-sunnah" means: the way and the custom. His words, ﴿"Then you will never find any change in the way of God, nor will you find any alteration in the way of God"﴾, mean: [regarding] His punishment of the disbelieving deniers. In this there is a clear threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 35, verses 44–45:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them, though they were greater than them in strength? And Allah is not such as to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed He is ever All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾ ﴿And if Allah were to take people to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature. But He defers them until a specified term; and when their term comes, then indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants.﴾

When He threatened them, exalted is He, in the verse before it with the practice (sunnah) of the earlier peoples, and that He does not change it or alter it regarding the disbelievers, He made them stand in this verse before what they saw of that on the road to Syria and elsewhere, such as the dwellings of Thamud and the like. "Yu'jizahu" means it escapes Him and eludes Him. The "min" in His saying ﴿min shay'in﴾ ("of anything") is an emphatic, superfluous particle (ziyadah muakkadah). And ﴿'Alīman qadīran﴾ ("All-Knowing, All-Powerful") are two attributes fitting for this context, for with them nothing is beyond reach.

Then Exalted is He explained the reason for His respite toward whomever of His servants He granted respite: that this is only because the Hereafter lies beyond all things, and in it the recompense of every person is fully paid. Had Mighty and Majestic He been to requite sins in this world, He would have destroyed everyone. His saying ﴿min dābbah﴾ ("any creature") is hyperbole, and what is meant is the children of Adam, since they are the ones who are recompensed. It was also said that what is meant is the jinn, and it was said that what is meant is every creature that crawls among the animals, since most of them exist only for the benefit of the son of Adam and on account of him. The pronoun in ﴿ẓahrihā﴾ ("its back") refers to the earth, mentioned earlier; even if it had not been previously mentioned, it would have been possible in this context to clarify the matter, and it would be like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32] and the like. "The specified term" (al-ajal al-musamma) is the Day of Resurrection. The rest of the verse is a threat, and within it is a promise for the believers.

The commentary on Surah Fatir is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
